finding.claim: /preview fetches an arbitrary attacker-supplied URL server-side with no validation and returns the response status and first 500 bytes of body to the caller (non-blind SSRF).

trace.note: target = request.args.get("url", "") - attacker controls full URL including scheme, host, port, path
requests.get(target) - server-side fetch with the app's network position; follows redirects by default
jsonify({"status": resp.status_code, "body": resp.text[:500]}) - response content reflected to attacker, so the SSRF is non-blind

finding.guards_checked: None on this path. No scheme allowlist, no host or IP allowlist, no private/link-local/loopback blocking, no DNS pinning, no redirect control. The only bound is timeout=5 (availability, not access control). Note: requests supports only http/https adapters, so file://, gopher://, and similar schemes raise InvalidSchema; impact is limited to http(s) reachability from the server, including cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), RFC1918 hosts, and localhost services.

verdict.guard_found: none. /preview (app.py:13-17) has no scheme, host, IP, or redirect check between the source at app.py:15 and the sink at app.py:16. The only validation in app.py is the ALLOWED_HOSTS check at app.py:23-25, which is in the separate /partner route and does not cover /preview.
verdict.reason: app.py:15 takes the full URL from an unauthenticated query parameter, app.py:16 calls requests.get(target) with no validation, and app.py:17 returns resp.status_code and the first 500 bytes of resp.text to the caller, so the SSRF is non-blind as claimed.

finding.claim: /partner gates the fetch on a hostname allowlist, but the allowlist is checked only on the initial URL and the fetch then uses a different URL parser and follows redirects, so an allowlisted host that redirects to an internal address bypasses the check. Status is the only data returned, so this is mostly blind.

trace.note: host = urlparse(target).hostname - validator parses with urllib.parse, not the parser requests uses (urllib3)
if host not in ALLOWED_HOSTS -> 400 - exact-string membership check on api.partner.example / cdn.partner.example
requests.get(target) - fetcher re-parses the original string with urllib3, follows 3xx redirects by default, and re-resolves DNS by name
returns only resp.status_code, so response body is not reflected

finding.guards_checked: Exact hostname allowlist (app.py:9, 24) with urlparse().hostname. Checked: no scheme check (requests limits schemes to http/https in practice); no port check; no userinfo/fragment handling beyond urlparse; no redirect validation (allow_redirects defaults to True for requests.get); no DNS pinning or resolved-IP check. Unverified: whether urlparse and urllib3 disagree on any concrete input (for example backslash, '?', '#', or '@' forms from the expertise guide) on current CPython and requests versions. I could not run a local parser comparison because the permission was denied. Exploitability depends on the allowlisted partner hosts returning redirects to internal targets, or on partner DNS being attacker-influenced; neither is visible in this repo.

verdict.guard_found: app.py:23-24: urlparse(target).hostname is checked by exact set membership against ALLOWED_HOSTS = {"api.partner.example", "cdn.partner.example"} (app.py:9), and a non-match returns 400 before the sink at app.py:26. This is the closing guard the rubric defines.
verdict.reason: The trace lines (app.py:22, 23, 24, 26, 27) match the candidate's description, but exact hostname membership on the parsed hostname at app.py:24 blocks any non-allowlisted initial host before requests.get at app.py:26. The remaining claim, that an allowlisted host can redirect to an internal address, depends on partner-side behavior that is not visible in this repo and is not a bypass of the closing guard as defined; a parser disagreement between urlparse and urllib3 is also unverified.
